explanations.explanation: This feature detects the little “[ … ]( … )”-style and “[ˆn]”-style bracketed markup used for inline links, citations, footnotes and section references in Markdown/LaTeX technical documents.

This neuron seems to mark the single most content-bearing word in a standalone title or headline—i.e. the head noun/verb that names the core topic or action (subtypes, slows, recycling, crisis, wall, mice, etc.).
This feature detects runs of closing‐parenthesis tokens—i.e. clusters of “)” (often two or more in a row) marking the end of nested expressions or function calls across math and code contexts.

This feature flags those little parenthetical glosses or tags that immediately follow a term—e.g. acronym expansions, translations or alternate names, dates or classifications, source bylines, disambiguation labels, etc.—serving as brief explanatory or clarifying annotations.

This neuron fires on “boilerplate” or metadata labels in text—proper names and section‐header tokens (journal or website titles like Cureus or PokéCommunity, software/class names like class-dump, legal headings like PRESENT or ELEVENTH, license keywords like EXCEPTION/misrepresent) that appear in document headers, footers or license/section titles.

This neuron flags tokens that are part of section‐ or document‐level headings/titles—the capitalized names, labels or phrases that introduce new sections (e.g. article titles, recipe headings, function names, license banners, chapter/TOC entries, etc.).

This feature lights up on small “stance-taking” words—epistemic/discourse markers like intend, probably, guess, know, due, wish, Before, etc.—that signal the author’s attitude, plan or level of certainty about what follows.

This feature fires on tokens that serve as the “header” or first word of a new section/heading (be it a news headline, article title, code‐block label or topical sub-heading), marking the start of a distinct topical segment.

This neuron is essentially a character‐ngram detector that lights up on common word-ending sequences (i.e. the last few letters of a token). Across English, Italian, Portuguese, code identifiers, etc., it consistently peaks on 2–5-letter suffixes (–eds, –ing/-utting, –so, –uit, –ply, –et, –but, etc.), so it’s acting as a morphological “suffix” feature.
This feature flags numeric tokens conveying quantitative facts—counts, measures, ages, dates, rates—across diverse technical or factual contexts.

The common thread is that this neuron lights up on the little “linking” words that kick off your main predicate or relation in a news-style sentence.  Whether it’s an auxiliary or light verb (has, had, took, made), a simple preposition/adverb (behind, like, between, out), or even the “](” of a Markdown link, it marks the token that glues your subject to its event, object or modifier—that is, the head of the clause’s predicate.
This feature flags capital‐letter segments (single letters or short uppercase substrings) that form parts of acronyms, codes or proper‐noun tokens in technical/formal titles and entity names.

This neuron fires on the “root” segments of capitalized proper names (people, places, brands, etc.), picking out common name-formation substrings (e.g. “pett,” “bett,” “esh,” “ney,” “rocket,” “gork,” …) that recur as the core of surnames or toponyms.

This feature picks out evaluative or comparative language in scientific/technical prose—terms like comparing/compared, effect(s), responsiveness, advantages, efficacy, relationship, characterization or implications—that flag when a text is stating study objectives, contrasting methods or conditions, and reporting comparative outcomes.

explanations.explanation: This feature detects personal given names (proper‐noun first names) used as bylines or entity mentions in news‐style and informational text.

This feature fires on the numeral “1” when used as a position marker in ordered sequences or enumeration contexts—e.g. “Page 1 of 1,” “Image 1 of 1,” “Step 1 of 5,” lecture/slide numbers, legal case citations, recipe measurements, etc.—i.e. the first element index in structured listings.

This feature lights up on the initial capitalized span of identifiers or headings—e.g. the first chunk of a PascalCase name (Tracing → “Tr,” Evaluator → “Eval,” AutoField → “Auto,” Sprintf, Connect, Update, etc.) or the first word in a title/sentence (“When,” “One,” “!”). In other words, it marks the start of a code symbol or a capitalized lead-off word in technical text.
This neuron is a proper-noun detector: it lights up on name-like tokens (especially surnames or other capitalized entity subwords) across contexts.

This neuron lights up on the very first word of a new “block” or heading—be it a question opener (“What,” “How,” “Which,” “Today,” “Would”), the initial article in an answer (“A,” “This,” “Just”), or the first keyword in a code section (“package,” “import”). In other words, it detects segment-start tokens that mark the beginning of a new heading, question, answer, or code block.
This neuron fires on isolated single‐letter tokens in all‐caps—e.g. “J,” “R,” “G,” “C,” “V,” “K”—when they occur as initials, abbreviations or lone letters in product, person or model names.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is a word-start capital-letter detector: it lights up on small BPE chunks that begin a capitalized term (e.g. “Dev,” “Vor,” “Ver,” “Je,” “Ad,” “Ev…”), i.e. the initial subword of proper names and technical labels.

This feature seems to fire on the single most salient “topic” word in a technical Q&A post—i.e. the key command, file path or extension, version, API name, core verb or noun that defines the subject under discussion.

Here’s a concise concept summary for each highlighted feature:

• HG  
  Recognizes the UK postcode prefix “HG” (and its numbered districts HG1–HG5) referring to Harrogate-area mail zones.  

• LGBT  
  Captures the acronym LGBT in discussions of the LGBT community, rights, harassment and legal protections.  

• GLW  
  Detects the “GLW” abbreviation in corporate/legal contexts (e.g. GLW Broadband, Inc.).  

• Social  
  Marks the word “Social” when it heads programs or initiatives—most notably Social Security or branded social-maturity/index concepts.  

• SF  
  Identifies the “SF” prefix in product or brand names (e.g. limited-edition SF X t-shirts).  

• LDL  
  Triggers on “LDL” in biomedical settings referring to low-density lipoprotein and its receptor.  

• MHC  
  Captures “MHC” in immunology texts denoting major histocompatibility complex class II antigens.  

• GLUT  
  Recognizes the “GLUT” prefix in glucose-transporter gene/protein names (e.g. GLUT1, GLUT4) in cell-biology papers.

This neuron is essentially a “tail‐segment” detector—it lights up on the closing piece of a multi‐part expression.  In running text that means the particle “up” in phrasal verbs (end up, crack up, roll up, etc.), and in numeric or code contexts the last chunk of a hyphenated or dotted number (phone-number blocks, π-digits, years, product IDs, etc.).

The feature is a detector for the indefinite/demonstrative determiner “another” (and occasionally “this”) when it’s used to introduce an additional instance, event or alternative—e.g. “another way,” “another process,” “another uptick,” “this was posted”—across news, Q&A, code, and informal contexts.

This feature fires on the initial capital‐letter fragments of proper names and titles—i.e. the two- to four-letter prefixes that kick off entity names (people, brands, organizations, species, headings) in running text.

This feature picks out the uppercase prefix “Drop” wherever it appears as the leading substring of a compound token—whether in brand or product names (Dropbox, Dropwizard, Dropzone), UI/API components (DropDownList), or headings/commands (“Drop weight,” “drop-off”). In short, it signals the lexical pattern “Drop” at the start of a token.

This neuron simply detects the letter‐sequence “is” (often in all‐caps) as a standalone or subword token—whether it’s the copula “IS,” the ending “-is” of names (Francis, Pulis, Raspanti, etc.), the “IS” in acronyms/place names (Mississippi, San Francisco), or the “_IS” suffix in code identifiers (PRIME_IS_DIVISIBLE).

This feature fires on the typical “file‐header” comment block in code or docs—i.e. the boilerplate metadata at the top of a file (copyright YEAR tokens, long dashed/equals separators, section labels like “Description,” license preamble, etc.).

This neuron fires on BPE subtokens that mark the start of a new word‐ or morpheme-segment—especially after punctuation or hyphens—often in proper names, hyphenated compounds and alphanumeric codes (e.g. “Bl” in “Double-Blind,” “oz” in “Wozniak,” “8” in “utf-8,” “1” in “UH-1,” “Bon” in “Saint-Bonnet,” etc.).
This feature fires on words that signal a challenge, hardship or worsening condition—i.e. lexical cues of difficulty, stress, “tricky” situations or deterioration across varied contexts.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires whenever the model sees the single‐letter token “p” or “P” on its own (as a standalone symbol rather than embedded in a longer word)—whether it’s a page-number prefix (p.121), a math‐variable p(y), a URL/query parameter (?p=501), a plasmid or protein name (pWCS358, p40), a gene symbol (pfrA), a class name (Paginator), or any other context in which “p”/“P” is tokenized by itself.

This neuron lights up on action-oriented keywords in technical contexts—especially verbs and directive tokens (“apply,” “contrib,” “offer,” “trouble,” “LICENSE,” “devote,” etc.) that signal procedural steps, configuration directives, or the invocation of operations in code snippets, Q&A posts, and scientific abstracts.
This neuron fires on subword pieces that carry word-initial capitalization—i.e. the beginnings or internal segments of proper names and titles (people, places, brands, etc.).

This feature is a simple orthographic detector for the letter bigram “sw” (especially at the start of a token), which lights up on all sorts of names (Swanson, Swalwell, Swartz, Swann), sports/team words (Swans), code or library identifiers (Swift, Swifter, Swinject), swim‐related terms, etc.

Here’s a concise concept label for each highlighted-token feature based on its top activations and contexts:

1. Determ(1.000) → “Determination”: Marks the “Determination of …” construction in scientific titles, flagging papers that report analytical measurement methods.  
2. Direct(0.819) → “Direct …”: Captures the adjective “Direct” at the start of scientific‐method titles, denoting protocols or assays performed without intermediates.  
3. Ex-(≈0.814) → “Ex- prefix”: Detects the “Ex-” prefix in news headlines to signal a person’s former role or title (ex-minister, ex-FBI boss, ex-wrestler).  
4. –(0.774) → “Element-list hyphen”: Highlights hyphens linking chemical element symbols in multi-metal formulas or compositional lists (Fe-Ni, Co-Cu, etc.).  
5. Inter-(≈0.773) → “Inter- prefix”: Picks up words beginning with “Inter-” in scientific/medical contexts (inter-comparison, inter-observer, inter-ictal) indicating between-entity relationships or processes.  
6. trying(0.769) → “trying (gerund)”: Fires on the present-participle “trying” in first-person anecdotal narratives describing personal attempts or experiences.  
7. Pre-(≈0.750) → “Pre- prefix”: Highlights “Pre-” prefixes in cooking, physiology, policy or medical definitions (preheat, pre/postjunctional, pre-existing, pre-diabetes) marking “before” states or actions.  
8. impossible(0.749) → “impossible”: Flags the strong negative adjective “impossible,” denoting categorical infeasibility or absolute denial in technical discussion.  
9. determines(0.740) → “determines”: Captures the verb “determines” in research contexts, signaling sentences that specify factors or mechanisms that decide outcomes.  
10. decide(0.739) → “decide”: Activates on the verb “decide” in informal/advice writing, marking choice-making or decision-guidance language.
